content: The Rockefeller Drug Laws refer to a set of statutes in New York State Penal Law that govern the sale and possession of narcotic drugs. These laws were named after Nelson Rockefeller, the governor of New York at the time of their enactment. Governor Rockefeller, a strong advocate for the legislation, signed the bill into law on May 8, 1973. Under these laws, the penalty for selling two ounces (approximately 56 grams) or more of heroin, morphine, raw or prepared opium, cocaine, or cannabis (including marijuana, which is not chemically classified as a narcotic) or for possessing four ounces (approximately 128 grams) or more of the same substances was equivalent to the penalty for second-degree murder. This meant a minimum sentence of 15 years to life in prison and a maximum sentence of 25 years to life. The original legislation also proposed the same penalty for committing a violent crime while under the influence of these drugs, but this provision was ultimately removed before the bill was signed into law. The section of the Rockefeller Drug Laws that applied to marijuana was repealed in 1979 under Democratic Governor Hugh Carey. However, the laws continued to impose severe penalties for other substances, such as cocaine and Schedule I or II opiates. Both the New York and Michigan statutes faced significant criticism from across the political spectrum. Conservatives, such as William F. Buckley, and many in law enforcement opposed the laws, arguing that equating the non-violent crime of drug trafficking with murder was inherently unjust. Civil rights advocates also condemned the laws, asserting that they were racially discriminatory, as they disproportionately targeted African Americans and, to a lesser extent, Latinos. Michigan's version of the law was reformed in 1998, reducing the mandatory life sentence to a minimum of 20 years. In New York, significant reforms were enacted in 2005 through the Drug Law Reform Act (DLRA). This legislation replaced the indeterminate sentencing system of the Rockefeller Drug Laws with a determinate system and reduced mandatory minimum prison sentences for non-violent felony drug offenders. The DLRA also lowered the minimum penalty for the most serious drug charges (A-I felonies) from 15 years to life to 8 years in prison for offenders with no prior felonies. Additionally, the weight thresholds for the most serious possession offenses (A-I and A-II) were doubled, and individuals serving life sentences were allowed to apply for re-sentencing. Since 2004, the number of prisoners serving sentences for A-I narcotics felonies in New York has been reduced by more than half.
